For the BLM, this means using science and science-based tools to support decisions about public land uses. The challenge of managing public lands to sustain their health, diversity and productivity for use and enjoyment by present and future generations unfolds within dynamic socio-ecological systems , rapidly advancing technologies and increasing availability of large datasets, along with a climate crisis that requires action across the Federal Government . First among this action is listening to the science, whether the decision involves energy development, recreation, livestock grazing, mining, timber harvest or another use of public lands. We administer research through eight program offices, spanning a broad range of disciplines: Accelerator R&D and Production , Advanced Scientific Computing Research , Basic Energy Sciences , Biological and Environmental Research , Fusion Energy Sciences , High Energy and Nuclear Physics , and Isotope R&D and Production . The DOE Office of Science Early Career Research Program provides annual funding opportunities for outstanding early career scientists in the disciplines supported by the DOE Office of Science. Courtesy of the Quantitative Biosciences Institute at the University of California, San Francisco. By Rachel Fairbank Published September 1, 2026 Scientists have mapped a network of interacting proteins, to create a “blueprint” of some of the molecular changes that are associated with autism spectrum disorder. The developmental disability affects an estimated 1 out of every 31 people in the U.S., runs in families, and is highly heritable , suggesting a genetic component. However, the underlying biology is highly complex. Hundreds of variations in genes and the proteins they produce may be involved in autism. pages.text: Scientists found 20 Homo naledi in a cave. Why are they all female? | National Geographic HISTORY & CULTURE Scientists found 20 ancient hominins in a cave, and a mystery: Why are they all female? A new protein analysis of Homo naledi skeletons reveals a curious twist—none of them seem to have Y chromosomes. Researchers have excavated hundreds of Homo naledi bones from the cave system known as Rising Star, including around 150 teeth, which can be used to determine the sex of skeletons. They now suspect that the majority of the individuals at the site were biologically female. By Helen Thompson Photographs by Robbie Shone Published June 24, 2026 Around 300,000 years ago, a cave in South Africa became the final resting place of at least 20 human cousins from the ancient species Homo naledi . Today, researchers have determined that all of those individuals appear to be missing a Y chromosome—the telltale genetic marker for males—and are likely female. Using a new method for sampling ancient teeth, the team was able to collect chemical clues about the sex of each skeleton without destroying it. The technique has the potential to “transform paleontology for several decades,” says Lee Berger , who is the National Geographic Society's Explorer in Residence, paleoanthropologist at Wits University in South Africa, and a co-author on the new study. Berger and his colleagues first discovered Homo naledi ’s bones in the cave system called Rising Star in 2013. Shaking up your exercise routine can help—and it might just increase your chance of living longer too. While it’s well documented that exercise lowers your associated mortality risk , few studies so far have investigated whether or not diversifying your exercise matters. But according to a new Harvard University study, in the long term, exercise variety makes a significant difference in longevity, regardless of how long you sweat. The participants logged their total time spent on multiple physical activities, including gardening, biking, running, strength training, tennis, climbing stairs, and yoga. It can then transmit information about the digestive tract to a reader outside the body. MIT News Ingestible sensors provide a helpful way to monitor a person’s health from the inside. But finding effective ways to power them has been a challenge. They typically use either standard batteries, which contain harmful chemicals, or external sources that provide energy wirelessly. Now, scientists have created digestible, paper-based batteries that can power medical devices inside the body and eventually get broken down. The technology, described in the journal Nature Chemical Engineering on September 21, has so far been tested only in pigs. If further studies confirm its safety in humans, it could one day power all sorts of medical devices. “For many of the systems we’re developing, we need power, and we power the system through different ways,” says study co-author Giovanni Traverso , a mechanical engineer at MIT and gastroenterologist at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, in a statement . “Often, we use batteries, so the question here was: Could we develop a battery that was bioresorbable, and then apply that across a range of application areas?” Bioresorbable Batteries for Transient Ingestible Bioelectronics Watch on The battery contains electrodes made with the metals magnesium and molybdenum, which are safe for human consumption in small amounts. Researchers have identified a cluster of sleep-related traits linked to more severe depression, offering new insights into how the body's internal clock may influence mental health and treatment. Anthony Hutchings By Nicholas St. Fleur Published October 30, 2025 One of paleontology’s most polarizing problems is a teenage Tyrannosaurus rex with an identity crisis, and two scientists say they’ve solved it. In 1942, researchers from the Cleveland Museum of Natural History found the skull of a small theropod in Montana’s Hell Creek Formation. After scientists classified it as the new species Nanotyrannus lancensis in 1988, the skull sparked four decades of fierce debate: Do such fossils of small and slender tyrannosaurs represent a teenage version of the fearsome T. rex , or an entirely distinct dinosaur? In a few places near the city of Talara, the oil seeps through fissures in the ground, creating mud-colored pits of gooey asphalt. During the Late Pleistocene, around 15,000 years ago, these tar pits were death traps that ensnared giants like ground sloths and dire wolves. Fin McCreath's 112, his first international century, helped the hosts post 281-7 at Forthill. Canada hit 50 inside eight overs thanks to Yuvraj Sumra (78), but they fell to 181-7 only for a partnership of 84 by Ansh Patel and captain Saad Bin Zafar to take them close to their target before George Munsey's catch secured Scotland's win with four balls remaining. Scotland are now assured a place at next year's Qualifier as Canada cannot catch them in the League 2 standings. It was the first game of the tri-series, which also involves the United Arab Emirates, to beat the wet weather after two washouts. Sarah Bryce, captaining the side in the absence of her sister Kathyrn, led the way with an unbeaten 70 as the hosts chased down their target of 130 in just over half of their allotted 32 overs, in a game which was originally scheduled for Sunday but fell foul of the weather. The Dutch had enjoyed a 58-run win in Glasgow on Friday and this was another one-sided contest. Darcy Carter made an early breakthrough, taking the wickets of Netherlands openers Phebe Molkenboer and Sanya Khurana, who had piled on more than 150 in last week's encounter. Abtaha Maqsood also took two quick wickets to leave the visitors reeling on 39-4. Maqsood struck again but Babette de Leede made 58 before being run out, while Caroline de Lange added 20 on the way to their total of 129-9. Scotland lost Maryam Faisal after four balls but Carter (33 not out) and Bryce made sure of a comprehensive success. pages.text: Scotland coast to win over Ireland as both reach Super Six phase - BBC Sport Image source, ICC/Getty Images Image caption, Kirstie Gordon took four wickets for just four runs in Dubai Published 18 November 2026 ICC Women's Emerging Nations Trophy Ireland 71 (19.3 overs): Lewis 20; Gordon 4-4, Maqsood 3-15 Scotland 72-2 (8.3 overs): Carter 30, Fraser 21 Scotland win by eight wickets Scotland's bowlers made short work of Ireland in a comfortable eight-wicket victory as both teams progressed to the Super Six stage at the Women's Emerging Nations Trophy in Dubai. Kirstie Gordon ripped through the Irish top order, the left-arm spinner taking four wickets for just four runs. Abtaha Maqsood claimed three wickets, Kathryn Bryce struck twice and Priyanaz Chatterji picked up her 50th T20 International wicket as Ireland were dismissed for just 71. Captain Gaby Lewis top scored for Ireland on 20, with Georgina Dempsey (12), Abbi Harrison (11) and Jane Maguire (11*) the others to reach double figures. In reply, Darcey Carter (30) and Katherine Fraser (21) enjoyed a 53-run opening partnership, with Kathryn Bryce (7*) and Sarah Bryce (4*) steering Scotland home in the ninth over. Scotland finished second behind unbeaten Sri Lanka in Group A, with Ireland in third place. Netherlands and Pakistan are guaranteed passage from Group B as Zimbabwe and Bangladesh vie for the remaining spot. pages.description: The BBC agrees an exclusive deal to broadcast live all Scotland men's international football matches in the run-up to the 2026 World Cup.
pages.text: Scotland men's internationals to be shown live on BBC - BBC Sport Image source, SNS Image caption, Live coverage of Steve Clarke's Scotland starts with a visit to Greece Published 7 March 2025 The BBC has agreed an exclusive contract to broadcast live all Scotland men's international football matches in the run-up to the 2026 World Cup. It is part of a wider deal agreed with European governing body Uefa that also includes matches involving Northern Ireland and Wales - the first time the broadcaster has secured live rights for all three of the UK's devolved nations. The contract includes all 14 live Scotland matches, beginning with the first leg of the Nations League play-off in Greece on 20 March and including June friendlies against Iceland and Leichtenstein as well as World Cup qualifiers. Director BBC Scotland Hayley Valentine said: "I'm so excited that millions of Scotland fans will now be able to enjoy free-to-air access to all Scotland's international matches. pages.text: Scotland propose Titwood venue for 2030 T20 World Cup - BBC Sport Image source, SNS Image caption, Titwood has been the home of Clydesdale Cricket Club since 1876 Published 11 November 2026 Glasgow's Titwood has been chosen as the proposed Scottish venue for the ICC Men's T20 World Cup in 2030. Home of Clydesdale Cricket Club since 1876, the ground is in the Pollokshields area of the city. The board of Cricket Scotland say their decision came following "engagement and consultation with the ICC, ECB and other strategic partners". The 2030 World Cup is being co-hosted by England & Wales, Scotland and Ireland. It will be the first major tournament in Scotland since the 1999 Cricket World Cup when The Grange in Edinburgh staged two group matches. Titwood would require a major overhaul and the next steps include talks with the Scottish and UK governments. Scotland's women met the Netherlands in a one-day international at Titwood in August, while the men played six T20 internationals there in June 2025. pages.title: Scotland women beaten by Sri Lanka in second Emerging Trophy group fixture - BBC Sport
pages.description: Scotland women succumb to a four-wicket defeat by Sri Lanka in their second Emerging Nations Trophy Group A fixture.
pages.text: Scotland women beaten by Sri Lanka in second Emerging Trophy group fixture - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Published 13 November 2026 ICC Women's Emerging Nations Trophy Scotland 111-8 (20 overs): Carter 62; Masqood 3-18 Sri Lanka 115-6 (18.1 overs): Gunaratne 49; Kumari 2-15, Sandeepani 2-18 Sri Lanka win by four wickets Scotland succumbed to a four-wicket defeat by Sri Lanka in their second Emerging Nations Trophy campaign Group A fixture. Having opened with victory over Papua New Guinea, the Scots batted first against Sri Lanka but were restricted to 111-8 in Ajman, United Arab Emirates. Darcey Carter top scored on 62 runs off 55 deliveries while Sathya Sandeepani and Sugandika Kumari took two wickets each. Sri Lanka's Vishmi Gunaratne amassed 49 runs off 41 deliveries, with captain Harshitha Samarawickrama contributing 24. Abatha Masqood took three wickets, becoming the Scots' top wicket taker in WT20Is, her 77 surpassing current captain Kathryn Bryce. Ten nations are participating in the UAE, split into two groups of five before a Super Six stage to determine the final on 25 November. Scotland play the hosts next, with UAE having opened with defeat by Ireland, who picked up a first win. Twelve years on from his debut - off the bench in a Poland friendly - he surpassed his friend and fellow Liverpool legend, Kenny Dalglish, whose record haul had stood for 40 years. In this role, he oversees a multi-billion-dollar portfolio dedicated to advancing the commercial deployment and scaling of innovative energy, materials, and industrial manufacturing technologies. His leadership supports CMEI’s mission to secure stable domestic supply chains, strengthen American manufacturing, and steward federal resources to provide affordable, reliable, and secure energy for the nation. Scott Pappano Scott Pappano Scott Pappano currently serves as the Principal Deputy Administrator of the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA). Mr. Pappano has dedicated nearly 35 years of service to the United States Navy as a submarine officer and acquisition leader, including at the rank of Vice Admiral before retiring in May 2025. Throughout his career, Mr. Pappano not only commanded at sea, but shaped the future of undersea warfare and strategic deterrence for generations to come. Pappano served onboard five submarines, including command of USS Buffalo (SSN 715) while forward deployed in Guam. Assignments ashore included submarine tactics development, Navy nuclear power training, defense international security policy, and Navy programming. After selection as an acquisition professional, Pappano served as Major Program Manager for the Strategic and Attack Submarine Program Office (PMS 392). pages.text: Scottish football could pave way for 3pm TV blackout to end - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Games currently cannot be shown live between 2:45pm and 5:15pm on a Saturday By Dale Johnson Football issues correspondent Published 29 October 2026 The first tentative steps to end the 3pm television blackout have been taken by Scottish football as it seeks offers for the next broadcast cycle. The SPFL has said that it is "flexible about the number of games" that will form part of the new deal, which will kick in from the 2029-30 season. BBC Sport understands this includes the possibility that broadcasters could bid to show all matches live - including those shown on a Saturday afternoon. The SPFL has created a tender with the greatest flexibility on the basis that the broadcaster does not seek to impose Article 48 of the Uefa Statutes. Article 48 allows leagues to set specific times when matches are banned from being shown live on television. It can only be enforced when 50% of matches in a country's top two divisions are played at the same time. While other parts of Europe have experimented with a blackout, it is now only present in the UK between 2:45pm and 5:15pm on a Saturday. Other leagues now tend to stagger kick-off times so the top divisions do not all play at the same time, meaning the blackout could not be applied. In the UK, 3pm remains the traditional, default kick-off time for all leagues from the very top down through non-league. SCIENCE LAELAPS Scrappy Fossils Yield Possible Dinosaur Blood Cells By Riley Black Published June 16, 2015 • 8 min read Last week, a little movie called Jurassic World debuted. You might have heard something about it . Paleontologists certainly have been jawing about it for a while, particularly how the movie’s dinosaurs stack up against the actual animals emerging from the rock.* But all the arguments about enfluffled dinosaurs and bunny hands have missed a more fundamental issue – could scientists ever recover enough intact dinosaur goo to populate a real Jurassic World? When the first Jurassic Park premiered in 1993, finding non-avian dinosaur DNA seemed a certainty. Two days before the official release of the movie Raúl Cano and colleagues announced that they had sequenced the DNA of a 135-120 million year old, amber-encased weevil. Woodward and colleagues announced that they had sequenced DNA from an 80 million year old dinosaur bone fragment. It seemed that life had found a way. Screening for Type 1 Diabetes Apr. 17, 2026 Key points Type 1 diabetes develops in stages and may start a long time before a person needs insulin. People at high risk for type 1 diabetes can benefit from screening before symptoms appear. Knowing they’re in the early stages of type 1 diabetes can help people notice symptoms and avoid serious complications. Who should be offered screening? People with a family member who has type 1 diabetes are 15 times more likely to develop type 1 than the general population and should be offered screening. It’s important to note, though, that most people who develop type 1 don’t have a family member with the condition. Screening can begin at 2 years old. Why get screened? Type 1 diabetes is often an emergency diagnosis. A person likely doesn't know they have type 1 diabetes until a serious complication happens, such as diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). pages.text: Sea turtles are surviving—despite us | National Geographic By Craig Welch Photographs by Thomas Peschak 25 min read This story appears in the October 2019 issue of National Geographic magazine. To see all that’s hopeful and appalling about the way we treat sea turtles , there’s no better place to start than the Burj Al Arab Jumeirah hotel. This shimmering tower of blue and white glass is shaped like the jib of a sailboat bound for shore. It rose two decades ago on an artificial island amid the steel forest of construction cranes that is Dubai, part of the United Arab Emirates. A royal suite, at 8,396 square feet, comes with a private cinema and 17 pillow options. A weekend stay can top $50,000. I have come here, though, to see its nonpaying guests. ( Saving Sea Turtles) Passing a fleet of white Rolls-Royces, I meet British expat marine biologist David Robinson. We take an elevator down to a parking garage and walk by Lamborghinis to our destination: a labyrinth of pipes and plastic pools, the intensive care unit of an elaborate marine turtle hospital. In one tub a green sea turtle struggles with internal organ damage. One floor up, sick, critically endangered hawksbills fill aquariums. Blood seeps from a dying leatherback harpooned by an indigenous hunter near Indonesia’s Kei Islands. Leatherbacks are the largest of the seven sea turtle species and one of the most imperiled. The West Pacific population has fewer than a thousand females. A flatback sea turtle kicks up sand while digging a nest on Crab Island, off Australia’s northeast coast. Plasynski, Ph.D. Sean I. Plasynski, Ph.D — Director, NETL Sean I. Plasynski, Ph.D., leads the complete NETL complex, including two major components: (1) world-class research and development (R&D) concentrated on energy technologies with a focus on hydrocarbons and geothermal energy and (2) development and implementation of a broad spectrum of national energy programs for the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) offices of Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy (formerly the Office of Fossil Energy); Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation; Electricity; and Cybersecurity, Energy Security and Emergency Response. Plasynski leads NETL's workforce of more than 1,800 people, located at three sites across the nation and an additional field office, who are responsible for R&D projects that span the United States. As laboratory director, Plasynski fosters strategic relationships with academic institutions, state and local governments and important energy industry stakeholders. Since joining NETL in 1992, Plasynski has held numerous management and technical positions, including principal deputy director, deputy director and chief technology officer, chief operating officer, director of the Strategic Center of Coal and sequestration technology

Try again ADVANCED SEARCH DOCKET SEARCH Search Home > Search Tips Search Tips To use this search page, you can look for a single word. Or, use the tips below to refine your search to find more specific results. In all these examples please note that the searches are case insensitive, so searching for Supreme Court is the same as searching for SUPREME COURT. Look for two or more words at once by just separating them by a space or using the AND operator. Example - type Supreme AND Court or simply Supreme Court to find documents that have both the word supreme and the word court anywhere. Look for a phrase. Example: type "Supreme Court" in quotes to find the exact phrase Supreme Court . The search is not case-sensitive. Look for words that are close to each other by using the NEAR operator instead of the AND operator. When you use NEAR, the closer together the words are, the higher the rank of the page, so the higher it appears in the list of search results. Example - type Rehearing NEAR denied to match documents where the word rehearing and denied are within 50 words of each other. Look for synonyms or similar words by using the OR operator. Note that if you don't use the OR operator and search using multiple words, a boolean AND operator is assumed. Example - type Order OR Journal to find documents containing the word Order or the word Journal , but not necessarily both. Limit your search by using the NOT operator to exclude words. Example - type surfing NOT
